fr:mainmatter.html:p: Coln is a database with an expressive language for schemas, queries, and migrations. This document forms the manual for Coln.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The entire manual is meant to be kept in a single global hierarchy rooted at the home page.
The Coln manual is an authoratative, conceptual, and incomplete reference document for engaged users and developers of Coln.
When the manual makes a definitive statement about the behavior of Coln, if the code deviates from the manual then the code is considered to have a bug.

There may be points in the manual where as I am writing, I decide that the current behavior of Coln is inadequate. In these places, I will write down what I intend the behavior to be, and mark the sentence with todo at the end.

The purpose of the manual is to produce understanding. The manual is not a specification, but a motivated reader could probably fill in the full details of a specification from the understanding imparted in the manual. Most importantly, a user of Coln who has carefully read the manual should not need to guess at what any particular piece of code means; the conceptual understanding laid out in this manual should be sufficient to give an unambiguous human-comprehensible semantics.
This manual (like Coln itself) is currently incomplete.
The Coln manual is not a tutorial. The Coln manual is not a place for original mathematical research. The Coln manual is not a development log.

Moreover, the Coln manual is not an advertisement. The intended audience of this manual is a reader with patience and a good amount of time, who is motivated for reasons found elsewhere to learn about Coln. There may be sections where we outline the rationale for a design decision; these should not be interpreted as claims of the superiority of this design decision, merely as a record of the thought process that went into it.

The Coln manual is written in Forester. Forester is a very flexible tool that can be used in many ways. In order for the manual to achieve its goals, it is necessary to put constraints on the use of forester.

We use a single address namespace without prefixes, similar to The Stacks Project. This means that creating new pages requires obtaining a “global lock” on the “next address” counter. Currently, Owen is holding this global lock; when more people are working on the manual we will coordinate around address allocation.
The entire manual is meant to be kept in a single global hierarchy rooted at the home page.
The manual contains a combination glossary and index, which collects technical terms used throughout the manual.

This manual is meant to be a single document with a single voice. Therefore, we do not put author metadata on individual trees, and all trees are considered to have been written by the Coln project. Moreover, we omit dates on non-reference trees; the manual as a whole should be considered as current, and out-of-date trees should be edited or deleted.
More generally, the Coln manual should be thought of as more of a Hyperbook than a Zettelkasten.
There are a variety of intended audiences for this manual; a given reader may fall into several of the following categories.
The categorical logician is a reader who is comfortable with modern approaches to the categorical semantics of type theory, such as:

fr:link.title: Categorical logic from a categorical point of view

html:li.fr:link: Categorical logic from a categorical point of view

fr:link.title: Type-Theoretic Signatures for Algebraic Theories and Inductive Types

html:li.fr:link: Type-Theoretic Signatures for Algebraic Theories and Inductive Types

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The categorical logician also has a reasonable grasp of topos theory and 2-category theory.

The type theorist is a reader who is comfortable with traditional type theory rules given in Gentzen’s tree notation and who might also have some experience with normalization by evaluation, but who is not yet familiar with the modern approaches of The categorical logician.

The database engineer is a reader who does not necessarily know any type theory, but is familiar with SQL, Datalog, Conjunctive queries, Egglog, Automerge, and perhaps some of the methods for incrementalizing queries like DBSP.
The developer is someone who is interested in contributing to Coln, or creating a Coln-like system.

The programmer-user is a reader who intends to incorporate Coln into a larger application. The programmer-user should be familiar with the language that they intend to use Coln from (currently, this is only TypeScript), and should be willing to learn a new language. We say “programmer-user” to distinguish this audience from the user of an application that the “programmer-user” creates; this user needs not read this manual.

The programmer-user who also falls into the earlier categories will benefit from a deeper understanding of Coln. However, Coln is also comprehensible in a self-contained way, just as one does not need to understand cartesian closed categories in order to use lambda x: x + 1 in Python, and it is a goal of this manual to present a clear conceptual picture for the non-mathematical programmer-user.
At various points in the manual we clarify which audience a certain section is for; a reader not in that audience may safely skip that section.
Coln can work as a little proof assistant which is restricted to positive types, but the real point of this restriction is to enable a translation to the database world.
One could look at this in two ways, depending on whether you think of the language or the database as “primary.”

In one sense, because the database engine can be used to reason about models defined purely in Coln, the database engine is essentially a souped-up tactic (in the sense of Rocq or Lean) for enumerating the elements of types.

But not all models of Coln theories need to be defined in Coln itself. As we have seen, the automatically-produced TypeScript functions can be used to initialize and populate a model in an imperative style. For instance, when using Coln to do an egglog-style analysis of a C-like language, one would first write a parser and type checker in a normal programming language, and then issue mutations via the API to create a model that represented the IR of the program. Then Coln queries could be run against that IR to resolve questions about the behavior of the program.
Thus, Coln is not a typical proof assistant; Coln is a tool that is meant to be integrated into a larger program that is not written in Coln.

In order to give the programmer a mental model for how they can expect these commands to work, in this section of the manual we describe the translation from a theory in the Coln language to a collection of tables.

Models of Coln theories are stored as collections of tables. For the reader experienced with traditional relational databases, tables should be fairly familiar, but we will go through them explicitly in order to establish our own conventions.
A table consists of a set of row IDs and a collection of columns. A table may come along with constraints, and in particular primary key constraints

Row IDs are an opaque type to the user, kind of like pointers without pointer arithmetic. In particular, a row ID may be dereferenced to look up the corresponding row in the database, and row IDs may be stored in columns to link tables together, but the content of a row ID is not meant to be meaningful or even stable.

This is becasue row IDs may exist in different formats in-memory, on disk, and over the network, and moreover may be subject to garbage-collection-like algorithms periodically in order to improve storage properties of the database.

A column is a sequence of values of some fixed data type, like String, Bool, Int, or RowId. Columns store one value for each row ID of the table they belong to, and they store these values in such a way so that it is efficient to access the corresponding value for each row ID. This could be achieved by storing the row IDs in sorted order, and storing the values in each column in the same order, so that a binary search over row IDs would produce the right index to access the column value at, but it is also possible that row IDs take the values 0,\ldots ,n-1, and columns may be directly indexed by row ID; the choice of how precisely this achieved is not something that is relevant at this level of abstraction.

As users do not interact with columns directly, we can identify the columns in a table by a simple sequential numbering 0,\ldots ,k-1; we call the number assigned to a column in this fashion its column index.

A primary key constraint is specified by a subset K \subseteq \{0,\ldots ,k-1\} of column indices. For each K-indexed tuple of values, a table satisfying the primary key constraint may have at most one row with columns assigned as in that K-tuple.

This can be used in a variety of ways. If K = \{0,\ldots ,k-1\}, then the table is a proper relation. If K = \{0,\ldots ,\ell -1\}, then K is a partial function from the first \ell column values to the last k - \ell column values.
A table with no primary key constraint can be thought of as a bag.
As a degenerate case, a table with no columns and a primary key constraint of \{\} has either zero or one row IDs.

Tables also have associated constraints. We discuss these in greater detail once we talk about how Coln theories are lowered to a collection of tables; essentially the constraints are what enforces the type dependencies between the different arguments to a function.
The key idea in translating a Coln theory into a usable database schema is that we can distribute records over functions. To understand this idea, first consider Coln theories of a special form.
A theory is in \Sigma \Pi normal form if a record type never appears in the codomain of a function type.

fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory Graph := sig vertex : Set edge : vertex -> vertex -> Set end

fr:title.text: Bag of graphs is not in \Sigma \Pi normal form

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Bag of graphs is not in \Sigma \Pi normal form

fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory BagOfGraphs := sig graph-id : Set graph-for : graph-id -> Graph end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Because Graph is a record type and it appears in the codomain of graph-for, BagOfGraphs is not in \Sigma \Pi normal form.

If a theory is in \Sigma \Pi normal form, it is fairly straightforward to represent it as a collection of tables. Specifically, ignoring the type dependency for now, each function type is of the form A1 -> A2 -> ... -> AN -> B, where A1,...,AN are all sets, and B is either a set, Set, or Prop. Then

html:ul.html:li: If B is a set, then we can represent this as a table with columns A1,...,AN,B and a primary key constraint on A1,...,AN.
If B is Set, then this is a table with columns A1,...,AN and no primary key constraint.
If B is Prop, then this is a table with columns A1,...,AN and a primary key constraint on A1,...,AN.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Thus, the first job to do when translating a Coln theory into a database schema is to put the Coln theory in \Sigma \Pi normal form.

fr:title.text: Bag of graphs in \Sigma \Pi normal form

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Bag of graphs in \Sigma \Pi normal form

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We can put BagOfGraphs in \Sigma \Pi normal form and then convert back and forth between the normal and original representations in the following way.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre:
theory BagOfGraphs/normal := sig graph-id : Set graph-for/vertex : graph-id -> Set graph-for/edge : (i : graph-id) -> graph-for/vertex i -> graph-for/vertex i -> Set end
def from-normal (m : BagOfGraphs/normal) : BagOfGraphs := struct graph-id := m.graph-id graph-for := i => struct vertex := m.graph-for/vertex i edge := v0 => v1 => m.graph-for/edge i v0 v1 end end
def to-normal (m : BagOfGraphs) : BagOfGraphs/normal := struct graph-id := m.graph-id graph-for/vertex := i => m.graph-for i .vertex graph-for/edge := i => v0 => v1 => m.graph-for i .edge v0 v1 end

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In this way, although when writing down BagOfGraphs it appears as if we would store a separate graph database for each graph id, in fact all of the graphs are stored in the same pair of tables. In particular, allocating a new graph id does not imply allocating a whole new graph structure.

There is a fairly straightforward algorithm to take a general theory to a theory in \Sigma \Pi -normal form, producing the from-normal and to-normal migrations simultaneously, but describing it here would involve a conceptual framework around the elaborator which would take a while to get off the ground. Thus, we ask the reader to take as given that we have access to such an algorithm, and we continue on assuming that we are working with theories in \Sigma \Pi -normal form.
One way of thinking about this algorithm is that it is a generalized version of the array-of-structs to struct-of-arrays transformation in, for instance, Zig's MultiArrayList.

For example, BagOfGraphs produces

Specifically, g0 has its own vertex and edge tables, but g1 merely “forwards” into the vertex and edge tables for all of the graphs in bog, (recall BagOfGraphs/normal from Bag of graphs in \Sigma \Pi normal form).
The next step after Distributing records over functions is to transform a set into pairs of a base type and validity predicate.
Recall from Record types as sets the query jealousy-triangle defined by
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def jealousy-triangle (m : Drama) : Set := tuple a b c : m.person m.jealous-of a b m.jealous-of b c m.jealous-of c a end

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A traditional database language (or indeed general-purpose language) has many syntactic classes used for different purposes.
SQL has an exceedingly large grammar. For instance, a single SELECT statement has many possible clauses, each with their own syntax (see the postgresql manual).

Many languages have a different syntax for type parameters to a function than regular parameters. For instance, in Rust one uses Vec<i32> for applying the Vec : Type -> Type function to i32 while normal function application looks like plus(1, 2), in OCaml one uses int list while normal function application looks like plus 1 2.

Coln differs from this, perhaps to an extreme degree, by only having essentially one syntactic class: the syntactic class of an element of a type. Even types themselves are in this syntactic class, because types are elements of type universes. What is achieved via syntactic differentiation in other languages is achieved instead by semantic restrictions in Coln.

In Coln there are set-level types, theory-level types, and top-level types. These all use the same syntax; operations which only work on set-level types will produce an error during elaboration. See Basic types for more information about this topic.

One downside of this approach is that the grammar of Coln is not a very meaningful way of getting a feel for the language; the grammar is almost trivial. What is important is understanding the semantics of Coln and the process of elaboration.

Elaboration is the process of producing syntax from notation, reporting diagnostics to the user when the user’s intent as expressed through notation is not compatible with the rules of the type theory.
Syntax is a data type in the Coln compiler, the elements of which are a compressed form for correct derivations in the Coln type theory.
The process of elaboration ensures that any syntax produced does in fact refer uniquely to some derivation.
Notation is another data type in the Coln compiler. Notation is the first “tree-shaped” data type that is produced in the compilation pipeline, and is fairly permissive in terms of what is allowed.
See fnotation for a description of the notation used in Coln.
A diagnostic is a message from the compiler to the user intended to explain a failure on the compiler’s part to fully understand the user’s intent.

Sometimes, there is a reasonable guess that the compiler can make as to how to continue, in which case the diagnostic is a “warning”—a warning that perhaps the choice the compiler is making is not what the user intended. In other cases, the compiler cannot make a reasonable guess, and the diagnostic is an “error”.

Coln follows the philosophy of Bicameral, Not Homoiconic in using a fairly unstructured “lower house syntax” as the target of parsing (or as Krishnamurthi calls it, “reading”). We use the term “notation” as a shorthand for “lower house syntax” in order to reserve the word “syntax” for trees that compactly refer to derivations. Unlike a traditional LISP, we do not use s-expressions. Our notation is instead inspired by modern LISPs like Julia and Rhombus. We call it “f-notation” for no particular reason.
In this section, we describe f-notation.
Lexing chops up a string into tagged chunks. F-notation has the following token kinds, which we break up into categories.

A name is built up out of a sequence of name segments separated by slashes with no intervening spaces. Each name segment is comprised either of alphanumerical letters or of symbols. Hyphens may appear in symbolic name segments or alphanumerical name segments. Only the last name segment in a name may be symbolic. Examples: Monoid/is-commutative, List/::.
The slashes are eventually intended to be used for namespacing in the style of yuujinchou; this is currently not supported however.
The f-notation configuration assigns special token kinds to specific name segments.

html:tr.html:td: Alphanumerical keyword, used for reserved words that nonetheless parse normally
Symbolic identifier, used for variables, defaults to infix application
Symbolic keyword, used for reserved infix keywords that nonetheless parse normally
Used to designate a top-level declaration
Used to modify a top-level declaration

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In Coln, the special name segments and their corresponding kinds are as follows.
Names with no segment found in the above list are classified as identifiers; it is invalid to have a multi-segment name that uses a reserved name segment.
We use boldface for block tokens and decl tokens in code snippets as a very rudimentary form of syntax highlighting.
Putting . in front of a name turns it into a field, and putting ' in front of a name turns it into a tag.
Fields are intended for use in accessing a record. For instance a .b gets the b field from the record; a.b is also valid and parses the same.
Tags are intended for use in creating elements of a sum type. For instance 'just 1 could be an element of the sum type Maybe Int. Currently Coln does not have either sum types or tags, however.
F-notation has string literals with double quotes and integer literals with arabic numerals.
There is a token kind for each of (, ), [, ], {, }, ,, ;, \n, and end-of-file.
When a certain token fails to lex for whatever reason, an error token kind is inserted and lexing continues.
Whitespace is generally ignored, though newlines create \n tokens.
Line comments starting with # are considered whitespace.
From tokens, the tree structure of f-notation is fairly simple. We give the main syntactic constructs here.
Most things in f-notation are expressions, including:
The exception is declarations which may only appear in blocks; a block contains statements which are either declarations or expressions. However, a block is an expression.
Identifiers, keywords, literals, tags, and fields are all expressions.
A tuple consists of an opening bracket followed by comma-separated expressions, followed by a closing bracket. For example: [a,b,c].
Juxtaposition is two expressions next to each other, like f x. As a.b lexes as two tokens, a and .b, this is also a juxtaposition.
Infix application is two expressions with a symbolic identifier or keyword between them, like a : Int.

Juxtaposition binds tighter than infix application and left associates. Thus, f x y is (f x) y and f x + y is (f x) + y. The binding strength and associativity of infix application is determined by a custom precedence table.
The precedence table for Coln is as follows.
The only role of parentheses in f-notation is to clarify binding, so in particular parentheses are always idempotent. That is, (e) is always the same as ((e)) in every context.
A declaration consists of a declaration token followed by an expression. For example
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def x : Int := 5
fr:mainmatter.html:p: is a declaration, which could be parenthesized as
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def ((x : Int) := 5)
fr:mainmatter.html:p: A declaration may be modified as well by modification tokens, as in
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: pub def x : Int := 5
fr:mainmatter.html:p: These modifiers form part of the overall declaration.
A block consists of a block token followed by either

html:ul.html:li: A newline, and then a sequence of newline-separated statements, closed by an end token.
An opening curly brace, and then a sequence of semicolon-separated statements, closed by a closing curly brace.todo

fr:mainmatter.html:p: An example of the first variant is
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: sig x : Int def x-plus-1 := x + 1 y : is-odd x-plus-1 end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: An example of the second variant is
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: sig { x : Int; def x-plus-1 := x + 1; y : is-odd x-plus-1 }
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Blocks may appear within expressions, but declarations may not; declarations may only appear within blocks.
The top level of a f-notation file is considered to be inside a block of the first variant, so it consists of a sequence of newline-separated statements.

At its core, there are only two things in the Coln language: types and elements of those types. We write a : A to express that a is an element of the type A. In this section, we describe informally the various types in Coln and how they are functionally involved in the database.

fr:title.text: Theories are schemas, models are instances

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Theories are schemas, models are instances

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In Coln, we use the word theory to mean a type used as a database schema, and we say model to refer to an element of a theory, which you might also think of as a database instance on the schema described by that theory.

We now show how to build up progressively more complex theories via different type formers. In order to give an intuition for what each of these type formers means, we also describe how to interact with models of those theories via the TypeScript FFI (note: the TypeScript FFI is a work in progress at the moment).
Set is a theory, and models of Set are collections of things. This corresponds to a very simple kind of database by itself, but we can do many things from this foundation.
We refer to models of Set as, unsurprisingly, “sets.”
In TypeScript, models of Set store collections of Values, where Value is defined in the following way
All elements in the collection should be of the same type (e.g. all row ids, all strings, etc.) but for simplicity all sets share the same untyped API involving Values.
A TypeScript value m that refers to a model of Set satisfies the following interface
If m has read-write permissions, then it will also satisfy the interface

Intuitively, add() does not take parameters because it adds a fresh element to the set, an element not equal to any other previous element. This means that a set of integers can never be read-write because it is impossible to create a fresh integer. We will see later on that it is instead possible to store a subset of the set of all integers; this will look differently however.
For a set with read-write permission, the following code should not throw an error.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: const a = m.add() assert(m.has(a))

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Records types are a way of composing multiple theories into one theory. A record type has multiple fields, each of which is declared to be a model of another theory. For instance:
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory SantaList := sig naughty : Set nice : Set end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: SantaList is a very simple theory, the models of which consist of a pair of a collection of naughty things and a collection of nice things.

More precisely, if we have a model m of SantaList in TypeScript, then m.naughty and m.nice are both models of Set. If m is readonly, then m.naughty and m.nice will satisfy ReadonlySet, and if m is read-write, then m.naughty and m.nice will satisfy ReadWriteSet. The following TypeScript code should run without errors if m is a read-write model of SantaList.
A model A : Set may itself be used as a theory. A model of A is just an element of A (remember that a model of Set is a collection of things). For example, consider the following theory.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory PopulatedSantaList := sig list : SantaList john : list.nice mary : list.naughty end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: A model m of PopulatedSantaList consists of a model m.list of SantaList, along with specific elements m.john in m.list.nice and m.mary in m.list.naughty.
In TypeScript, an element of a set comes along with a getter, and if it is read-write, also a setter. So if m is a TypeScript variable accessing a model of PopulatedSantaList, then we should have:
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: assert(m.list.nice.has(m.john.get()))
fr:mainmatter.html:p: If m is incomplete, then m.john.get() might return null. This would be the case in a freshly-created model, as in
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: const m = PopulatedSantaList.create()
fr:mainmatter.html:p: This can be remedied by using .set(), as in
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: const john = m.list.nice.add() m.john.set(john)
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Note that m.john.set(x) would throw an exception if x were not in m.list.nice.
Function types are theories, as long as the domain is a set and the codomain is a theory.
Function types can be used in many ways. Here are some examples.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory StateMachine := sig state : Set next : state -> state end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: If we have m : StateMachine, then m.next is a function that sends elements of m.state to other elements of m.state. The type state -> state satisfies the criterion for being a theory because its domain is a set and its codomain is a theory (following Sets as theories). Concretely, in TypeScript, we could use this like
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: const m = StateMachine.create() const [x,y] = [m.state.add(), m.state.add()] m.next(x).set(y) m.next(y).set(y)
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Note that at the point where we have added x and y but not yet set the values of next for them, m is not a valid instance for StateMachine. In fact, in general it is inevitable that in the process of building a model one may pass through an invalid state. Thus, validity is only checked at certain points; we discuss validity more in a later section.todo
But that is not all functions can do. As the codomain of a function can be a theory, we could also do the following.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory SantaLists := sig year : Set list : year -> SantaList end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: From TypeScript, we could use a model m of SantaLists in the following way.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: const y2025 = m.year.add() const bob = m.list(y2025).nice.add()
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Now, there are some ontological problems with this database schema. We cannot ask whether a person is nice one year and naughty the other year, because the nice and naughty sets for each year are disjoint. What we would really like is there to be one set of people, and then in different years they might be nice or naughty. This can be accomplished with relations.

There is a theory Prop which is even more boring than Set; it is the theory of a set with at most one element. One could think of it also as a truth value: inhabited means true and empty means false. From TypeScript, we have the interface

While on its own Prop is boring, we can combine it with function types to make it more interesting. For instance, we can now rewrite SantaLists so that the same person may appear on lists in different years.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre:
theory SantaListOver (person : Set) := sig naughty : person -> Prop nice : person -> Prop end
theory SantaLists := sig year : Set children : Set list : year -> SantaListOver children end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Here we have also introduced an additional feature: a theory can have parameters, which are models of other theories. In this case, SantaList now takes in a parameter person which is a model of Set. We instantiate this parameter with children in SantaLists.
In TypeScript, we could interact with a read-write model m of this new SantaLists in the following way.
We call a function whose codomain is Prop a relation. m.list(y2025).nice is a unary relation because it takes in one argument. Here is another example, this time of a binary relation.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory Drama := sig person : Set jealous-of : person -> person -> Prop end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: From TypeScript, using a model of Drama would look like:
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: const [john, mary] = [m.person.add(), m.person.add()] m.jealous_of(john)(mary).makeTrue()
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Note that because names in fnotation can contain characters like - that are not allowed in TypeScript, we have to mangle the Coln name to create the TypeScript API. As person_of is also a valid name in Coln, a theory could have both person-of and person_of fields. In this case, emitting the TypeScript FFI would emit an error. The suggested fix is to not have fields that differ only by choice of hyphen/underscore, because that is bad and confusing in any case.

Just like a set is a theory, a proposition is also a theory; a model of the proposition can be thought of as a witness that the proposition is true. We can use this to put laws in our database. For instance, we can make jealousy be transitive.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory ExtraDrama := sig person : Set jealous-of : person -> person -> Prop jealous-of/is-transitive : (a b c : person) -> jealous-of a b -> jealous-of b c -> jealous-of a c end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: We saw earlier one way in which a model of a theory might be incomplete; a function might not yet be defined for given values of its inputs. Here we have a similar situation. For instance, we might have written:
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: const [john, mary, sue] = [m.person.add(), m.person.add(), m.person.add()] m.jealous_of(john)(mary).makeTrue() m.jealous_of(mary)(sue).makeTrue()
fr:mainmatter.html:p: When checking validity of m after executing this code, Coln will report that jealous-of/is-transitive john mary sue _ _ : jealous-of mary sue is not satisfied (though, Coln does not know what names we have given to these variables in TypeScript, so it would actually print out the row identifiers instead of the names).todo Unlike with next in the section on functions, to fix this we don't need to touch jealous-of/is-transitive. Instead, we can just run m.jealous_of(john)(sue).makeTrue(), and the model will be valid again. This is because if the codomain of a function is a proposition, there is ultimately only one possible way for that function to exist, and thus the function need not be explicitly defined. We discuss how this works in a later section.todo
Another way of creating interesting propositions is with equality. Given two elements a0 and a1 of a set A, there is a proposition a0 = a1 which is true if and only if a0 is equal to a1.
We can use this to write down laws in our theories that involve equality. For instance, we can write down the theory of a two-way mapping (mathematically known as a bijection) in the following way
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory TwoWayMapping (X : Set) (Y : Set) := sig fwd : X -> Y bwd : Y -> X bwd-fwd : (x : X) -> bwd (fwd x) = x fwd-bwd : (y : Y) -> fwd (bwd x) = x end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Another example of equality usage is when we assert that a relation is a partial function, by saying that if x is related to both y0 and y1 then y0 must be equal to y1.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory IsPartialFunction (X : Set) (Y : Set) (R : X -> Y -> Prop) := (x : X) -> (y0 y1 : Y) -> R x y0 -> R x y1 -> y0 = y1
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Equality is useful for constraints, but is especially useful for queries.

These six type formers (The theory of sets, Record types as theories, Sets as theories, Function types as theories, Propositions and relations and Equality types as theories) can be used to compositionally build up fairly complex combinatorial structures of sets, functions and relations. However, they are still limited when it comes to handling data, which often has, for instance, numbers and strings in it.

We could simply put in String and Int in as “base sets”. However, this would permit functions String -> String, and we cannot store a function like that in a database because the set of strings is infinite and the function must be total, so storing the value of the function at every string would take infinite storage. We could say that String was a theory and not a set, which would prevent it from being used in the domain of a function, but it is perfectly sensible to have the theory String -> Prop (which denotes a subset of the set of all strings), and making String a theory would prevent us from forming that.

The solution to this problem requires building up a little more theory, so we do not address it right now, and instead continue on to give a full account of the “purely combinatorial” fragment of Coln.

fr:title.text: Sets are queries, elements are results

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Sets are queries, elements are results

fr:mainmatter.html:p: One can query a database in Coln via for-loops in TypeScript, but this is obviously not the most efficient or ergonomic way to do it. In fact, we already have the machinery to write down queries, it just requires a bit of rethinking what we have already learned. The idea is that giving a way to produce a set from a model of a theory is a query. The elements of that set are the results of the query.

Just like we have record types as the theory-level, we also have record types at the set-level. We can use this to define a set in the context of a model of a given theory; this is how to “natively query” an instance of a Coln theory.todo
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def jealousy-triangle (m : Drama) : Set := tuple a : m.person b : m.person c : m.person a-b : m.jealous-of a b b-c : m.jealous-of b c c-a : m.jealous-of c a end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: In TypeScript, jealousy-triangle is compiled to a function that takes in a model of Drama and returns a ReadonlySet.todo The elements v of this ReadonlySet are Values with the "tuple" tag, which have fields a,b,c that are elements of m.person, such that m.jealous-of(v.value.a)(v.value.b).isTrue(), and so on. The value v will also have v.value.a_b, but it will just be null, thought of as the unique element of the singleton set.

Iterating through the elements of jealousy_triangle(m) will be faster than the naive approach of a triply-nested for-loop over m.person and then filtering out using m.jealous-of, because Coln can plan the query and take advantage of fast join algorithms on the m.jealous-of table.todo
This query can be written more compactly in the following way.todo
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def jealousy-triangle (m : Drama) : Set := tuple a b c : m.person m.jealous-of a b m.jealous-of b c m.jealous-of c a end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: We can omit the field names for propositions because we never need to refer to the witnesses of the propositions, we just need the propositions to be true.
As a variation on the same theme, we could look for length-3 cycles in a state machine with
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def next-triangle (m : StateMachine) : Set := tuple a b c : m.state m.next a = b m.next b = c m.next c = a end

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In the queries, we saw several usages of the pattern
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def query (m : T) : Set := ...
fr:mainmatter.html:p: def is in fact a much more general construct; any theory can replace Set on the right, and we can take in multiple arguments.
In general, this allows one to create a view of a model one theory, in the form of a model of another theory.

fr:title.text: Elements of record types as views

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Elements of record types as views

fr:mainmatter.html:p: If a theory is given by a record type (using sig ... end), then we can produce a model of it using struct ... end, setting all of its fields. For example, we can reward the wrong children with the following code (using SantaList from Record types as theories).
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def santa-mixup (m : SantaList) : SantaList := struct naughty := m.nice nice := m.naughty end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: When using struct, one must give all the fields of the original record type in the same order as they were originally defined.
With some slightly more complex code, we can produce a model of SantaList from a model of SantaLists and a choice of year.

Intuitively, this assigns naughty to the set of children naughty in that year, and similarly with nice. The tuple syntax is just as in Record types as sets, using the curly-brace inline syntax. And m.list y .naughty child is just a sequence of function applications and field projection. Walking through the types, we have m.list : m.person -> SantaListOver m.person, so m .list y : SantaListOver m.person and then m.list y .naughty : m.person -> Prop and finally m.list y .naughty child : Prop.

fr:title.text: Elements of function types as views

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Elements of function types as views

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Just as we can produce elements of record types with struct ... end, we can produce elements of function types with lambda syntax x => a, just like anonymous functions in Javascript.
As an example, we can produce the graph of a function, which is a binary relation on the domain and codomain.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def graph (X : Set) (Y : Set) (f : X -> Y) : X -> Y -> Prop := x => y => f x = y
fr:mainmatter.html:p: We can also now start making some non-trivial views of theories that involve function types. For instance, we could run a state-machine at double speed.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def double-time (m : StateMachine) : StateMachine := struct state := m.state next := x => m.next (m.next x) end

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In Basic types we learned:

html:ul.html:li: How to use theory and def. These are the only two top-level declarations in Coln, so we have now learned all of the top-level declarations.
How to use Set, Prop, sets, record types, function types and equality types to build up theories.
How to produce some models of theories from other models.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In Inductive types, we will see how to produce more models of theories, which will in turn allow us to produce more theories. However, the basic structure introduced here will remain more or less the same.
An interesting fact about Coln as a language the reader may have noticed is that the only model of Set that one can write down in the empty context is the singleton type tuple {}.

This is remedied by inductive types. In Coln, inductive types are produced by initial models. An initial model for a theory T is a model of T that makes zero decisions: the only elements in the sets in the model are the ones forced to exist by the laws of the theory.
Recall from Sets as theories the theory PopulatedSantaList given by
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory PopulatedSantaList := sig list : SantaList john : list.nice mary : list.naughty end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: We can define JohnAndMary to be an initial model of PopulatedSantaList in the following way.todo (Note that here the type of JohnAndMary is inferred to be PopulatedSantaList).
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: ind def JohnAndMary := init PopulatedSantaList
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Now JohnAndMary is a model of PopulatedSantaList where JohnAndMary.list.nice is a set that only contains JohnAndMary.john and JohnAndMary.list.naughty is a set that only contains JohnAndMary.mary.
The empty set is the initial model of Set.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: ind def empty := init Set

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We can use initial models in order to take the transitive closure of a graph in the following way.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre:
theory Drama := sig person : Set jealous-of : person -> person -> Prop end
theory TransitiveExtension (@ind m : Drama) := sig transitively-jealous-of : m.person -> m.person -> Prop include : (x y : m.person) -> m.jealous-of x y -> transitively-jealous-of x y transitive : (x y z : m.person) -> transitively-jealous-of x y -> transitively-jealous-of y z -> transitively-jealous-of x z end
ind def TransitiveClosure (m : Drama) := init (TransitiveExtension m)
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Given a model m of Drama, we can then access the transitive closure of m.jealous-of via TransitiveClosure m .transitively-jealous-of. The intuition here is that init (TransitiveExtension m) give us the minimal binary relation that both extends m.jealous-of and also is transitive; this is precisely the transitive closure.
We discuss why @ind m is necessary shortly.
While initial models are very powerful, they must be used carefully. First of all, not all theories have initial models.

fr:title.text: The theory of a point does not have an initial model.

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The theory of a point does not have an initial model.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: As sets are theories, we might try to produce a point of any set via the following definition.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: ind def something-from-nothing (A : Set) : A := init A
fr:mainmatter.html:p: However, this would make Coln inconsistent by allowing us to produce a point in the empty set.

Intuitively, we can not take an initial model if that would involve producing “out of nothing” elements of sets that are already defined. We can only introduce elements into sets that are in the process of being defined.
This also means that if a theory has a function whose codomain is an inductively-defined set (a set defined as part of an initial model), there is no initial model for that theory.

fr:title.text: A theory with no initial model

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A theory with no initial model

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We can define Or in the following way.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre:
theory Or/motive (@ind p0 : Prop) (@ind p1 : Prop) := sig implicand : Prop impl0 : p0 -> implicand impl1 : p1 -> implicand end
ind def Or (p0 : Prop) (p1 : Prop) : Prop := init (Or/motive p0 p1) .implicand
fr:mainmatter.html:p: We call it Or/motive for reasons we will get into later; broadly speaking the motive is the theory one needs to provide a model of in order to use an element of Or p0 p1.
Intuitively, Or p0 p1 is the minimal proposition that is implied by both p0 and p1. Then the following has no initial model.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory HardChoice := sig likes-bananas : Prop likes-apples : Prop at-least-one : Or likes-bananas likes-apples end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Intuitively, struct { true; false; _ } and struct { false; true; _ } are both models of HardChoice, but neither one is “more minimal” than the other, and the only way to get something “more minimal” than both would be struct { false; false; _ } but this is not a model of HardChoice.
In fact, this theory would be rejected by the Coln type theory. In order to make Coln accept this theory, one must put ind in front of theory, as in
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: ind theory HardChoice := sig likes-bananas : Prop likes-apples : Prop at-least-one : Or likes-bananas likes-apples end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Then this is a perfectly fine schema for a database, but we cannot take an initial model of an “inductive theory”. Sometimes we say “conjunctive theory” to refer to the normal theories, of which it is possible to take initial models.
Give more examples of initial models, explain @ind, talk about how to use element of types in initial models.

This page collects technical terms used throughout the manual. Some of these terms refer to specific projects, some of them refer to more general concepts. Via the backlink system of Forester, this also serves as an index; going to the page for any entry in the glossary gives the reader a list of sections in the manual that reference it.

We have chosen to put projects in the glossary rather than as bibliographic items because of the nature of projects as ongoing and evolving rather than static, moreover in the software world the distinction between a concept and the flagship software which implements that concept can sometimes be blurry. Additionally, as this is a manual and not an academic document, the primary function of references is breadcrumbs-to-learn-more not attributions-of-credit; thus the link given is often Wikipedia or the nlab.
ACSet stands for “attributed C-set” and is pronounced with the Hungarian “cs” which is the English “ch.”

html:ul.html:li: Paper: Categorical Data Structures for Technical Computing

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In the above nlab page, we follow the definition of “arithemetic universe” as a list-arithmetic pretopos.
DBSP is a language for “describing computations over data streams.” It is defined in DBSP: Automatic Incremental View Maintenance for Rich Query Languages, and currently implemented in Feldera.
A derivation is a sequence of applications of rules in some type theory, starting from the empty premise and concluding in a judgment.

See Rule of inference on wikipedia for an introduction to this sort of thing. The only difference is that a derivation in type theory typically expresses that there is a term of a certain type rather than just expressing that a proposition is true.
A principled approach to derivations may be found in Categorical logic from a categorical point of view.
See also the rhombus paper.
SQL, or “Structured Query Language”, is a family of languages used to declaratively access relational databases.

In this section, each section is a relatively self-contained introduction to some of the math or design philosophy behind Coln. The start of each section specifies which audience the section is intended for.

fr:title.text: Type theory as a language for anything

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Type theory as a language for anything

fr:mainmatter.html:p: (This is meant for The type theorist, The database engineer, The developer, The programmer-user)

A programmer with a passing familiarity with type theory may have formed some preconceptions about what a type is, and what it means to give an element of that type. For instance, in a language like Haskell or Rust, types are how we put structure on pieces of computer memory, so that we remember that the value at a certain address is a pointer or integer or floating point number. In a proof assistant, types are used as a foundation for mathematics; types play the role of the “sets” that informal mathematicians use.

The truth is that types do not have any intrinsic meaning. Rather, type theory is a convenient tool for working with any collection of things which relate to each other in certain precise, well-structured ways.
In particular, type theory is a tool for working with things defined by universal properties.
In set theory, if A and B are sets then to produce an element of A \times B it suffices to produce an element of A and an element of B, and vice-versa.
In propositional logic, if P and Q are propositions then to produce a proof of P \wedge Q it suffices to produce a proof of P and a proof of Q, and vice-versa.
In a programming language with tuple types, if a and b are types then to produce an element of (a,b) it suffices to produce an element of a and an element of b, and vice-versa.
In number theory, in order to show that k is a divisor of the GCD (greatest common divisor) of m and n, it suffices show that k is a divisor of m and n, and vice versa.
Again in set theory, if U and V are subsets of a larger set X, then to show that x is an element of U \cap V it suffices to show that x is an element of U and an element of V, and vice-versa.
In group theory, in order to produce a homomorphism from G to the product group H_0 \times H_1, it suffices to produce a homomorphism from G to H_0 and from G to H_1, and vice-versa.
This list could consider ad nauseum, but the reader should get the point by now; there's a pattern going on.
The concept of a universal property is formalized in different ways, often using category theory, but we need not bother with formalization at this stage.

The reader may have heard of “the Curry-Howard correspondence”, often informally referred to “propositions as types”. The Curry-Howard correspondence shows how various type formers and logical connectives correspond. With all due respect to Curry-Howard the name “correspondence” is somewhat of a misnomer because it assumes a false equivalence between the two things that are claimed to be in correspondence. In particular, propositional logic is a mathematical domain in which type theory may be applied to form a convenient syntax; it is by no means the only domain.

The reason type theory may be usefully applied to propositional logic because all of the connectives of propositional logic (and, or, not, forall, exists, etc.) satisfy universal properties; this is the same as the reason why type theory may be applied to any other area.

The way that type theory may be applied to a particular area is via the development of a particular type theory. Confusion between type theory as a subject and the concept of a type theory as a mathematical object is an unfortunate side effect of the nomenclature, because “ breaks with the convention that in group theory, we study groups, in field theory we study fields, or in category theory we study categories.

A particular type theory is merely a syntactic formalization of some collection of universal properties, consisting of a collection of rules by which we judge that a certain piece of syntax is well-typed. The beauty of universal properties is that each universal property is quite self-contained, so a type theory may be designed by systematically observing which universal properties the objects of interest support, and then adding the standard type-theoretic rules for those universal properties to one's type theory.

And this is the method that we have followed in order to design the type theory for Coln: observe the universal properties that our domain of interest (relational databases) satisfy, and add rules corresponding to these universal properties. Fortunately, the result of this systematic development seems to produce a language which expresses many of the important database operations.

fr:title.text: A type theory for geometric theories

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A type theory for geometric theories

fr:mainmatter.html:p: (This is meant for The categorical logician)

The ultimate intended semantics for Coln is in arithmetic theories, which are the analogue of geometric theories for arithmetic universes. However, geometric theories and topoi are both better-studied than arithmetic universes and are additionally closely related, so we give an exposition of the basic type theory in terms of geometric theories. Note that by topos we mean Grothendieck topos, not elementary topos, so in particular all topoi have natural numbers objects.

Following the principles of this manual, this is not a mathematical paper; there will be a more formal account of this type theory, but that is in progress. Rather, this is a conceptual account that makes reference to mathematics.
In The Elephant, Johnstone makes the following definitions for “theory”; we call this an elephant theory in order to distinguish it from other notions of theory we might consider.

For \mathcal {S} a topos, an elephant theory over \mathcal {S} is a (pseudo-)functor T \colon (\mathsf {BTop}/\mathcal {S})^\mathrm {op} \to \mathsf {Cat}, where (\mathsf {BTop}/\mathcal {S})^\mathrm {op} is the 2-category of bounded geometric morphisms into \mathcal {S} and \mathsf {Cat} is the 2-category of large categories.
A morphism of elephant theories is simply an indexed functor.

We say that T is classified by \mathsf {S}[T] \colon \mathsf {BTop}/\mathcal {S} if T is contravariantly represented by \mathcal {S}[T], that is T(\mathcal {E}) \cong \mathsf {BTop}/\mathcal {S}(\mathcal {E}, \mathcal {S}[T]). We also call \mathsf {S}[T] the classifying topos for T.
(See Elephant Definition B4.2.1)

The object classifier \mathbb {O} is the elephant theory defined by the forgetful functor (\mathsf {BTop}/\mathcal {S})^\mathrm {op} \to \mathsf {Cat} which sends a bounded topos over \mathcal {S} to its underlying category of objects.
(See Elephant Example B4.2.4(a))
If T is a geometric theory, then a geometric construct is a \mathsf {BTop}/\mathcal {S}-indexed functor F \colon T \to \mathbb {O}.
The idea is that F, given a model M of T in an \mathcal {S}-topos \mathcal {E}, produces an object of \mathcal {E}.
(See Elephant Definition B4.2.5)
Geometric theories may be consicely defined as the elephant theories built up via a sequence of product-inserter-equifier limits starting from the object classifier.
We expand this to give more intuition.

If T is a theory, a simple functional extension of T is another theory T' given as the inserter of two geometric constructs F,G \colon T \to \mathbb {O}. Intuitively, T' is the theory given by freely adding a new morphism between the “objects” F and G.

If T is a theory, a simple equational extension of T is another theory T' given as the equifier of two indexed natural transformations \alpha , \beta \colon F \Rightarrow G, where F and G are geometric constructs. Intuitively, T' is the theory given by adding a new equality between morphisms of “objects”.
A geometric theory is a theory built up by a finite sequence T_0,\ldots ,T_n of simple functional extensions and simple equational extensions starting from T_0 = \mathbb {O}^m for some finite m.

(See Elephant Definition 4.2.7, note that Johnstone gives a slightly different definition, using simple geometric quotients in place of simple equational extensions, which use inverters instead of equifiers. The name “simple equational extension” is not known to us to be previously used, but it follows the schema of “simple functional extension.”)
Any geometric theory has a classifying topos.
(See Elephant Theorem 4.2.9)

fr:title.text: A category with families structure on elephant theories

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A category with families structure on elephant theories

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Let \mathsf {ElTh} be the category of elephant theories. Then let \mathsf {Ty} \colon \mathsf {ElTh}^\mathrm {op} \to \mathsf {SET} be the large presheaf which sends an elephant theory \Gamma to the set of strict 2-functors A \colon (\int \Gamma )^\mathrm {op} \to \mathsf {Cat}.

Intuitively, \mathsf {Ty}(\Gamma ) is “elephant theories relative to \Gamma .” This is because \int \Gamma is the category of topoi equipped with a model of \Gamma ; if \Gamma were a geometric theory then \int \Gamma would be equivalent to \mathsf {BTop}/\mathcal {S}[\Gamma ].

Then define \mathsf {Tm} \colon (\int \mathsf {Ty})^\mathrm {op} \to \mathsf {Set} by letting \mathsf {Tm}(\Gamma , A) be the set of sections of A. A section a is a natural assignment of a(\mathcal {E}, M) \colon A(\mathcal {E}, M) for (\mathcal {E},M) \in \int \Gamma .

Context extension is given in the following way. Suppose that \Gamma \colon (\mathsf {BTop}/\mathcal {S})^\mathrm {op} \to \mathsf {Cat} is a context and A \colon \mathsf {Ty}(\Gamma ). Then \Gamma \triangleright A \colon (\mathsf {BTop}/\mathcal {S})^\mathrm {op} \to \mathsf {Cat} is defined by (\Gamma \triangleright A)(\mathcal {E}) = (M \colon \Gamma (\mathcal {E})) \times A(\mathcal {E},M).
Then finally we have weakening and the variable rule given by the first and second projections out of \Gamma \triangleright A.
Note that even though topoi and elephant theories are non-trivially 2-categorical, (\mathsf {ElTh},\mathsf {Ty},\mathsf {Tm}) forms nevertheless a strict (albeit quite large) category with families.
The remainder of this section is simply an investigation of what type formers are supported in \mathsf {ElTh}.
Coln is a tool for logical reasoning.

html:ul.html:li: Tool means that Coln performs routines that answers questions.
Logical means that these routines have well-defined mathematical semantics.
Reasoning means that the routines are meant to check and produce proofs (the questions: “is this proof valid?” and “is there a proof of X?”).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Coln is similar to both existing proof assistants and existing databases.

One way of looking at Coln is that it is the result of cutting out everything from a dependent type theory that can't fit in a database, and then seeing if database technology (query planning, efficient data structures) can speed up the process of proof search for the problems which are still expressible.

Another way of looking at Coln is that it is a dependently typed approach to databases, derived by first finding a denotational semantics for database languages and then using standard techniques to distill an internal language for that denotational semantics.

A third way of looking at Coln is that it is a module system for Egglog/Eqlog-style reasoning, similar to Modulog but using an approach to module systems more inspired by Pterodactyl and Logical Relations as Types rather than A modular module system.

A fourth way of looking at Coln is that it is an attempt to realize the vision of Steve Vickers for databases, which started with Geometric theories and databases but has continued on through, for instance, Sketches for arithmetic universes.

A fifth way of looking at Coln is that it is a proof assistant with first-class support for quotient inductive inductive types, in the sense of having quotient inductive inductive signatures as a first-class concept, and then allowing the formation of the initial models for these signatures and induction over those initial models.
A sixth way of looking at Coln is that it is Automerge for acsets.

The design of Coln embodies a thesis around a deficiency in current proof assistants: in non-well-structured domains (for instance, verification of machine code), it is hard to keep track of the vast quantity of tiny, trivial lemmas needed to prove some property. Mathematics as done by humans is often elegant, beautiful, and conceptually compressible, in that a proof involves a conceptual simplification of the problem domain and often naturally breaks up into theorems, definitions, lemmas that can be given fairly meaningful names and organized hierarchically.

However, the mathematics involved in a proof in a non-well-structured domain does not have this property, and if we want a systematic approach to organizing the lemmas then we should use a database that we can query in flexible ways, rather than relying on a naming convention.
But there are many roads to and from Coln; the core ideas are very elementary in a certain sense and we expect to be surprised by where Coln ends up being applicable or not applicable.
